passages.t: New tablets, an ark, and the tribe of Levi
passages.happening:
Moses finishes the story of the golden calf. After his prayer, God said, “Chisel out two stone tablets like the originals, come up to Me on the mountain, and make an ark of wood. And I will write on the tablets the words that were on the first tablets, which you broke” (verses 1-2).

Moses made the ark of acacia wood, cut the tablets and climbed the mountain. God wrote on them the Ten Commandments, as before. Moses came down and put the tablets in the ark, ‘and there they have remained’ (verse 5).

A short travel note follows. It records where Aaron died and was buried, and that his son Eleazar became priest after him (verses 6-7).

Then: “At that time the LORD set apart the tribe of Levi to carry the ark of the covenant of the LORD, to stand before the LORD to serve Him, and to pronounce blessings in His name” (verse 8). Levi has no share of land, for ‘the LORD is his inheritance’ (verse 9).

Moses stayed on the mountain forty days and nights, and God listened again and did not destroy the people (verse 10). He said, ‘Get up’, and sent Moses on ahead of them toward the land (verse 11).
passages.hearers:
Chapter 9 ended with Moses on his face and no answer given. This is the answer. God does not speak a word of pardon here. He tells Moses to cut new stone.

The first tablets lay in pieces at the foot of the mountain, the sign of a broken covenant. Now God writes the same words again. Nothing is taken out and nothing is made easier. The covenant is given back whole to the people who broke it.

The ark was a wooden chest, later covered with gold and carried on poles. In the ancient world a treaty was often kept in a holy place, sometimes at the feet of a god's statue, so that the god could witness it. Israel had no statue. Its copy of the covenant lay in the ark, under the place where God was said to sit as king. The ark was like the footstool of a king no one could see.

Verses 6 and 7 are set off in many translations as a note in brackets. Their point is plain from the context. Aaron had made the calf, and God had been angry enough to destroy him (9:20). Yet Aaron died an old man, long afterward, and his son served as priest in his place. The priesthood was not taken away.

The Levites were the tribe set apart for the worship of God. In a people where every family's living came from its land, they were given none. They lived on what Israel brought to God. What sounds like a loss is turned into an honor: the LORD himself is what they have.

Then, in verse 11, come two words that end the whole dark story: ‘Get up.’ The march to the land goes on.
passages.later:
Exodus tells the same moment: “Chisel out two stone tablets like the originals, and I will write on them the words that were on the first tablets, which you broke” (Exodus 34:1).

When Solomon brought the ark into the temple centuries later, “There was nothing in the ark except the two stone tablets that Moses had placed in it at Horeb” (1 Kings 8:9).

God had told Aaron what verse 9 says of his tribe: “I am your portion and your inheritance among the Israelites” (Numbers 18:20).
passages.hard:
Verse 6 says Aaron died at Moserah. Numbers says he died on Mount Hor. Which is right?

Numbers 20:22-29 and 33:38 place Aaron's death on Mount Hor. Numbers 33 also lists these camps in a different order from the one given here.

Readers have explained this in several ways. Some suggest that Moserah was the name of a district or camp at the foot of Mount Hor, so that both accounts describe one event. Some note that Numbers 33 is a list of camps, while these verses are a brief note added for another purpose, and that Israel may have passed through the same area more than once. Scholars who hold that the first five books draw on several sources take the passages as keeping different memories of the wilderness route.

Where Mount Hor and these camps lay is not known in any case, and these notes do not settle the question. The purpose of the note is clear. Even after the calf, God continued the priesthood through Aaron's son and set apart the Levites to serve him.
passages.asks: God answered the broken tablets by writing the same words again. Ask whether you believe God gives back what you have broken, or whether you expect a lesser version of his care from now on. And hear the two words of verse 11. Ask where, after a failure that has been forgiven, you are still sitting down when you have been told to get up.

passages.t: ‘What does the LORD your God ask of you?’
passages.happening:
Moses turns from the story to his hearers. “And now, O Israel, what does the LORD your God ask of you but to fear the LORD your God by walking in all His ways, to love Him, to serve the LORD your God with all your heart and with all your soul, and to keep the commandments and statutes of the LORD that I am giving you this day for your own good?” (verses 12-13).

He gives the ground for it. The heavens and the earth and all that is in them belong to God. “Yet the LORD has set His affection on your fathers and loved them. And He has chosen you, their descendants after them” (verse 15). So: “Circumcise your hearts, therefore, and stiffen your necks no more” (verse 16).

Then he says who this God is. “For the LORD your God is God of gods and Lord of lords, the great, mighty, and awesome God, showing no partiality and accepting no bribe. He executes justice for the fatherless and widow, and He loves the foreigner, giving him food and clothing” (verses 17-18).

And the command that follows from it: “So you also must love the foreigner, since you yourselves were foreigners in the land of Egypt” (verse 19).

Israel is to fear God, serve him and hold fast to him (verse 20). Their fathers went down to Egypt ‘seventy in all’, and now they are as many as the stars (verse 22).
passages.hearers:
‘And now’ marks the turn. After two chapters of Israel's failures, a hearer might brace for a heavy demand. What Moses gives is a summary: fear, walk, love, serve, keep. These are not five separate tasks. They are one life described from five sides, and all of it is ‘for your own good’.

The appeal moves in a pattern. Moses says something about God, and then says what follows for Israel.

First: God owns everything, the highest heavens and the earth, and still he set his love on this one small family. So, circumcise your hearts.

Circumcision was the sign of the covenant, carried in the body of every Israelite male since Abraham. Moses turns it into a picture of something inward. A heart can have a covering over it that makes it dull. That must be cut away so the heart can feel and answer. He ties it to the picture from chapter 9: do not be stiff-necked any longer. An outward sign without an inward change is not enough.

Second: God is the highest of all powers, and he cannot be bought. He does not look to see who is important, and he takes no bribe. A judge who favored the powerful or could be paid was a familiar evil in that world. And what does the God above all gods do with his power? He takes up the case of the orphan and the widow, and he loves the foreigner enough to feed and clothe him.

These were the three weakest groups in a society built on family land and male heads of households. A person with no father, no husband or no clan had no one to plead for them and no share in the land. Kings in Mesopotamia and Egypt boasted of protecting widows and orphans. Deuteronomy goes further. It says that God himself loves the foreigner, and it commands every Israelite to do the same.

So the second ‘therefore’: love the foreigner. The reason is memory. Israel knew from the inside what it was to be the outsider. Its own suffering is to make it kind.

This is a command to Israel about how its people were to treat those who lived among them. These notes draw no rule from it for any government or party today. They do say what it asks of every reader: the person near you who does not belong is to be loved.

The verb in verse 20, ‘hold fast’, is the word used in Genesis when a man holds fast to his wife. Loyalty to God is meant to be that close and that lasting.

The last verse sets a number beside a promise. Seventy people went down to Egypt. God had told Abraham to count the stars. Moses points at the crowd in front of him and says that it has happened.
passages.later:
The prophet Micah asks Moses' question again and answers it: “And what does the LORD require of you but to act justly, to love mercy, and to walk humbly with your God?” (Micah 6:8).

Jeremiah repeats the call to the heart: “Circumcise yourselves to the LORD, and remove the foreskins of your hearts” (Jeremiah 4:4). Later in this book God promises to do it himself (Deuteronomy 30:6). Paul says that this is what God does by his Spirit: ‘circumcision is a matter of the heart, by the Spirit, not by the written code’ (Romans 2:29).

Peter learned the truth of verse 17 in the house of a Roman officer: “I now truly understand that God does not show favoritism, but welcomes those from every nation who fear Him and do what is right” (Acts 10:34-35).

Leviticus gives the same command about the foreigner: “You must treat the foreigner living among you as native-born and love him as yourself” (Leviticus 19:34).

And Jesus, describing the last judgment, says, “I was a stranger and you took Me in” (Matthew 25:35).
passages.asks: Moses says that the God who owns the heavens spends his power on the orphan, the widow and the foreigner. Ask who is the person near you with no one to speak for them, and what it would mean to love that person and not only to be fair to them. And ask what is covering your heart, so that you hear these words and feel little.
